10 A stone is dropped from a tall building. Air resistance is significant. The variation of distance
fallen with time is shown by the dashed line.
A second stone with the same dimensions but a smaller mass is dropped from the same building.
Which line represents the motion of the second stone?
A
B
distance
path of first stone
C
D
0
time
0

hints: Notice the axes are distance fallen against time, so the gradient at any point is the instantaneous velocity $v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$ and both stones start from rest with zero gradient.
Connect same dimensions to air resistance: at any given speed $v$ the drag force is the same for both stones, but weight $W = mg$ is smaller for the second stone.

Compare terminal velocities where $drag = weight$: the lighter stone balances at a lower $v$, so its distance-time line must curve over to a smaller constant gradient below the dashed path of the first stone.
walkthrough: Identify the graph meaning: $y$ is distance fallen and $x$ is time, so gradient is velocity. Both stones are dropped, so both curves start at the origin with zero gradient and steepen as they accelerate.
State the force rule: resultant force $= mg - drag$. Same dimensions means drag depends only on speed in the same way, while smaller mass means smaller $mg$.
Explain terminal velocity: it is reached when $drag = mg$ and acceleration becomes zero. Because $mg$ is smaller, this equality happens at a smaller drag and hence a smaller velocity $v_T$.

Translate to the distance-time shape: after initial acceleration, each curve becomes approximately straight with gradient $= v_T$. The second stone must tend to a less steep straight section than the dashed line.

Check the options: A and B lie above the dashed line, meaning larger distance and larger $v_T$, which is opposite to the physics. D is far too flat. Only the line below the dashed line with a reduced but non-zero final gradient fits. This is option C.

A.explanation: Line A falls further in a given time than the first stone, implying a larger speed. A lighter stone cannot fall faster when size and air resistance are the same.

B.explanation: Line B is also above the dashed path of the first stone for most of the time, implying greater distance fallen. Smaller weight with the same drag cannot give a larger terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Same size gives the same drag at a given speed, but smaller mass gives smaller weight, so $drag = weight$ occurs at a lower speed. The distance-time gradient is therefore smaller at terminal velocity, lying below the first stone.

D.explanation: Line D shows almost no increase in distance, implying a terminal velocity far too small. The mass is only a little smaller, so the reduction in terminal velocity is modest, not almost zero.
